prerequisites: Elementary vector calculus. Concept of derivative and integral, with application to elementary functions.
System of linear equations and matrices.
Elementary concepts of kinematics and dynamics of the particle. Concept of force and Newton's principles. Work, kinetic and potential energy and energy conservation.
Kinematics and dynamics of the rigid body. Geometry of masses. Moments of inertia.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Ability to work in a team.
Understanding and mastery of basic concepts on the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, and electromagnetism and their application to solving engineering problems.
Knowledge of the principles of theory of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and kinematically synthesize mechanisms.
Pose and solve the direct and inverse dynamic problem of a planar mechanism.
Analyze and design rigid and flexible transmissions.
Know widely applied mechanisms and understand that many mechanisms, seemingly very different, respond to the same kinematic principles.
Create kinematic diagrams of real mechanisms as a form of representation and understand the mechanism's operation from said diagram.

Structurally analyze articulated mechanisms by criteria of nature and number of links or pairs, and by dimensional criteria, describing, as a consequence, the degrees of freedom or mobility of the mechanism and the existence or absence of dead or return points and their singularities.
Know and develop the concepts, fundamentals, and methods applied for the kinematic and dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Calculate velocities, accelerations, and forces in any planar mechanism, for specific positions of the mechanism and for complete cycles of movement.
Determine the type and dimensions of a bar mechanism to perform a specific function (problem known as mechanism synthesis).
Assimilate the relationships between the actions and the movement they produce in machines and be able to recognize the type of dynamic problem associated with each case.
Determine the inertia effects supported by the links or bars that make up the mechanisms.
Correctly include friction forces in sliding, rotational pairs, and rolling, and analyze and understand the operation of friction-based mechanisms.
Know and define the key dimensions and characteristics of motion transmissions between rotating shafts (gears, belts, ...).
Determine transmission ratios in ordinary and epicyclic gear trains and know the design criteria preferably used to define the number of teeth.
Describe the role played by cam mechanisms, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages in relation to other mechanisms that achieve the same results.
Use software for the analysis, simulation, and design of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and select information from various sources.
Develop the ability to understand and interpret the results obtained through kinematic and dynamic analysis of mechanisms and machines.

syllabus_topics: Mechanisms and machines. Basic concepts and schematization.
Definition, general structure, and components of a machine
Classification of kinematic elements and pairs
Mobility of mechanisms: Grübler and Kutzbach criteria
Articulated quadrilateral and kinematic inversion. Grashof's Law
Direct dynamic analysis on reduced mechanisms
Flywheels: Steady state, degree of irregularity, concept of GD2
Sliding friction, in rotational pairs and rolling friction.
Concept of balancing. Balancing of mechanisms.
Fundamentals, terminology, and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Cylindrical helical, bevel, and worm gears.
Fundamentals, terminology, and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Ordinary and epicyclic trains. Willis's formula.
Fundamental law of design and kinematics of cams.
teaching_methods: Laboratory / field / computer room / language classroom practices

assessment_methods.method: Continuous Assessment (EC): Problems performed in classroom practices and/or tasks proposed by professors.
Laboratory practices (PL): Preparation, attitude, submission of a report, and/or multiple-choice tests.
Final Exam (EF): Conceptual questions or quick-resolution problems, and problems similar to those in classroom practices.

assessment_rules: For the ordinary and extraordinary June calls, the final grade is calculated as EC + PL + EF, provided a minimum of 3 points out of 7.5 is achieved on the Final Exam (EF). If the minimum is not met, the final grade will be 4.9. For the extraordinary January call and differentiated evaluation, the assessment consists of a single written exam, where 9 points are for the subject's syllabus and 1 point for laboratory practice content; a minimum of 5 points out of 10 is required to pass. Grades from previous years are not carried over.
